Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verses 1–2:

﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾. That is, the verses of this surah. It may also mean the verses of the scriptures in general, and it may mean the Qur'an in general, though this last is far-fetched because the Qur'an is mentioned again after this. ﴿And that which has been sent down to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an. Its grammatical analysis (i'rab) is that it is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿the truth﴾. ﴿Without pillars﴾, meaning without any pillars that you can see, except the power of God. ﴿That you can see﴾. It has been said: the pronoun refers to the heavens, and on this reading ﴿that you can see﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) or is a new independent clause (isti'naf). It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the pillars, meaning that it has no visible pillars, which implies by inference that it has pillars that are not seen. The majority (al-Jumhur) said: it has no pillars at all, so the intended meaning is the negation of pillars and the negation of their being seen. ﴿Then He istawa upon the Throne﴾. Here "then" (thumma) indicates the order of reporting, not the order of occurrence, since the Throne existed before the creation of the heavens. The discussion of istawa has already been given in al-A'raf [7:53]. ﴿He arranges the affair﴾, meaning the affair of the dominion (malakut). ﴿He details the signs﴾, meaning the signs of His books.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 3:

﴿He spread out the earth﴾ implies that it is flat (basit) and not spherical (mukawwarah), and this is the apparent meaning of the Shari'ah. The notion of spreading and extension (al-bast wal-madd) may be reconciled with sphericity, because every piece of the earth is extended on its own, and sphericity applies only to the earth as a whole. ﴿And placed firm mountains﴾ means the steadfast mountains (al-jibal al-thabitah). ﴿And of every fruit He made in it two mates, two﴾ means two kinds of fruit: such as black and white, and sweet and sour. If it is said: the verse implies that God created two kinds from every fruit, yet He created many kinds from many fruits. The answer: that adds to the consideration (al-i'tibar) and is greater in demonstrating power, so He mentioned two, because the demonstration of other than two is a fortiori (min bab awla). It was also said: the sentence is complete at His words ﴿and of all the fruits﴾, and then He begins with His words ﴿He placed in it two mates﴾, meaning the male and the female. The first view is better. ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾, meaning He clothes it with it, so that it becomes for it like a covering (ghisha'), and this is a figure of speech (tashbih).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 4:

﴿Qiṭaʿun mutajāwirāt﴾ means: adjacent plots of land, lying side by side. Even though they are adjacent, their soil varies: some is good and some poor, some hard and some soft, and other differences. All of this is evidence of the Creator who chooses (al-Ṣāniʿ al-Mukhtār), who wills (al-Murid), and who has power (al-Qādir). ﴿Ṣinwānun wa-ghayru ṣinwān﴾: the ṣinwān (clustered palms) are palm trees that grow many together from one root, while ghayr al-ṣinwān (non-clustered) are those that stand separately, one by one. The singular of ṣinwān is ṣinw. ﴿Yusqā bi-māʾin wāḥid wa-nufaḍḍilu baʿḍahā ʿalā baʿḍin fī al-ukul﴾ is a proof and demonstration that He, exalted is He, is All-Powerful and All-Willing, because the difference in their taste, shapes, and colors, despite the water they are irrigated with being the same, is evidence of power and will. In this is a refutation of those who attribute things to nature (al-ṭabīʿa).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 5:

﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾ That is: if you are amazed, O Muhammad, then their denial of the resurrection is truly deserving of wonder, for the One who was able to create what we have mentioned of the heavens, the earth and the fruits is able to create creation again after their death. ﴿"When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ This is the saying of the disbelievers who deny the resurrection. The reciters differed regarding this passage and in all the passages that contain two interrogatives, and they are eleven passages: the first of them is this one; in al-Isra' there are two passages; in al-Mu'minun one passage; in al-Naml one passage; in al-'Ankabut one passage; in Alif Lam Mim al-Sajdah one passage; in al-Saffat two passages; in al-Waqi'ah one passage; and in al-Nazi'at one passage. Some of them recited with an interrogative in the first and the second, some recited with an interrogative in the first only, which is Nafi', and some recited with an interrogative in the second only. The original form of the interrogative lies in the meaning, and in such a passage it is really about the second. The interrogative particle's meaning is denial, and they denied that they would be a new creation, but they did not deny that they would be dust. So whoever recited with an interrogative in the second only, it is according to the original form; and whoever recited with an interrogative in the first, the intended interrogative is the second; and whoever recited with an interrogative in both, that is for emphasis. ﴿And those—the shackles are upon their necks﴾ It may be that he intends the shackles in the Hereafter, in which case it is literal; or he intends that they are prevented from faith, like your saying: ﴿Indeed, We have placed shackles upon their necks﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8], in which case it is metaphorical, running in the manner of sealing and setting seals upon the hearts.

They ask you to hasten the evil before the good (﴿وَيَسْتَعْجِلُونَكَ بِٱلسَّيِّئَةِ قَبْلَ ٱلْحَسَنَةِ﴾), that is, to hasten the punishment before the well-being. The meaning is that they demanded the punishment in a spirit of mockery. ﴿وَقَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِمُ ٱلْمَثُلَٰتُ﴾: "al-mathulat" is the plural of "muthla," on the pattern of "tamra," and it refers to a great punishment that makes a person an example (mathal). The meaning is: how can they ask for punishment when punishments have already befallen the nations that came before them? Do they not fear the like of that?

﴿وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَذُو مَغْفِرَةٍ لِّلنَّاسِ عَلَىٰ ظُلْمِهِمْ﴾: he means His concealing (of their sins) and His granting them respite in this world, for the disbelievers and the disobedient. It was also said: he means His forgiveness for whoever repents, but the first view is more apparent here.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 7:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ The verse: They proposed that a sign be sent down upon the Prophet ﷺ, such as an angel descending with him or something similar, and they did not take heed of the Qur'an or of the other great signs with which he came. This was from them a form of obstinacy. ﴿Indeed, you are only a warner﴾ That is, your duty is only to warn them, and it is not incumbent upon you to bring them a sign; that rests with Allah. ﴿And for every people is a guide﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions. The first is that the guide (hadi) is meant to be Allah the Exalted, so the meaning is: your duty is only the warning, and Allah is the Guide for whomever He wills, whenever He wills. The second aspect: he means by the guide the Prophet ﷺ, so the meaning is: you are only a prophet warner, and for every people there is a guide from among the prophets who warns them; thus your matter is neither novel nor objectionable. The third: it is related that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I am the warner, and you, O ʿAli, are the guide."

God knows what every female bears, as in His saying: He knows what is in the wombs. This is one of the five things that none knows but Allah. It means He knows whether it is male or female, complete or incomplete (khidaj, i.e. a miscarried fetus), good or bad, or other than that. ﴿And what the wombs diminish and what they increase﴾. The meaning of taghid (diminish) is to decrease, and the meaning of tazdad is to increase. It has been said that the reference is to menstrual blood, which decreases and increases. It has also been said that it refers to the child: ghayd is a miscarriage, or birth before nine months, and ziyada is its remaining in the womb for more than nine months. It is possible that "ma" in His saying "what every female bears" and "what the wombs diminish and what they increase" is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 10:

﴿Whether among you is one who conceals speech or one who speaks aloud, it is the same to Him.﴾ The meaning: indeed Allah hears everything, so loud speech and whispered speech are equal in His sight. In this and what follows there is a division (taqsim), which is one of the instruments of rhetorical expression (adawat al-bayan), for He mentions four categories. There is also in it a tibaq (antithesis): ﴿and one who hides himself by night and goes freely about by day﴾. The meaning: it is the same before Allah, the one who hides himself by night, who is in the utmost concealment, and the one who goes freely by day, who is in the utmost visibility. The word sarib means one who moves about freely in his sarb (with a fatha on the ra), that is, in his path and his direction. The sarib and the mustakhfi are two persons; the intention is to equate them in terms of Allah's knowledge of both, despite the difference in their states. It has also been said that "the one who hides himself by night and the one who goes freely by day" are two attributes of a single subject, who hides by night and appears by day. What supports this is his saying "and sarib," where he joins it by conjunction as attributes, and he did not say "and one who is sarib" with the repetition of "man" as he did in "whoever conceals speech and whoever speaks aloud with it." However, making them two is more preferable, so that it corresponds to "whoever conceals speech and whoever speaks aloud," and the division is thus completed into four on this reading. In that case, his saying "and sarib" is a conjunction to the clause, which is his saying "and one who hides himself," not to "mustakhfi" alone.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 11:

﴿لَهُ مُعَقِّبَٰتٌ﴾ "Mu'aqqibat" here refers to a group of angels, and they were called mu'aqqibat because some of them follow (ya'qubu) others. The pronoun in "lahu" refers back to "man" mentioned earlier, as if He said: for whoever conceals speech and whoever speaks openly, and for whoever hides himself and whoever shows himself, there are mu'aqqibat. It was said that it refers back to Allah, but this is a weak view, because the pronouns that follow it refer to the servant by agreement. ﴿يَحْفَظُونَهُ﴾ "They guard him" is a description of the mu'aqqibat, and this guarding may mean guarding his deeds, or guarding him and protecting him from calamities. ﴿مِنْ أَمْرِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ "by the command of Allah" is a description of the mu'aqqibat, meaning mu'aqqibat by the order of Allah, i.e., He commanded them to guard him. It was also recited as "bi-amri Allah," and this reading supports that interpretation, and according to this view "min amri Allah" does not relate to "yahfazunahu." It was said that it relates to it, meaning they guard him from the punishment of Allah if he sins, by their supplication for him and their seeking forgiveness for him. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لاَ يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ﴾ "Indeed, Allah does not change what is with a people," meaning of well-being and blessings, ﴿حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُواْ مَا بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ "until they change what is in themselves," meaning through sins. This implies that Allah does not take away blessings, nor does He remove calamities, except because of sins.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 12:

﴿He shows you the lightning, [causing] fear and hope.﴾ The fear comes from the lightning, from thunderbolts and other terrifying things, and the hope is for the rain that comes with ﴿the heavy clouds.﴾ He described them as heavy because they carry water. ﴿And the thunder glorifies [Him] with His praise.﴾ Al-Ra'd (thunder) is the name of an angel, and its audible voice is tasbih (glorification). It has come in a report that its voice is a driving-away of the clouds, so according to this, its tasbih is other than that. ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾: it was said that this refers to the thunderbolt that descended upon Arbad [ibn Rabi'ah], the disbeliever, and killed him when he and his brother 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ). But the wording is more general than that. ﴿And they dispute concerning Allah﴾: meaning the disbelievers. The waw is either for resumption (isti'naf) or for the circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿And He is mighty in strength (shadid al-mihal)⦆: that is, severe in power. Al-mihal is derived from al-hilah (stratagem), so the mim is augmental, and its pattern is mif'al. It was also said that its meaning is severe in plotting, from your saying "mahala bi al-rajul" when he plotted against the man, so the mim according to this view is original, and its pattern is fi'al, and the interpretation of "plotting" according to this view is like its interpretation in the places where it occurs in the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 14:

﴿To Him is the call of truth.﴾ It has been said: it is "There is no god but Allah" (lā ilāha illā Allāh). The meaning is that the calling of the servants in truth is to Allah, and their calling in falsehood is to other than Him. ﴿And those they call upon besides Him do not respond to them with anything,﴾ meaning by "those": what was worshipped besides Allah, such as idols and others. The pronoun in "yad'ūn" (they call upon) refers to the disbelievers, and the meaning is that the deities worshipped do not respond to those who worship them ﴿except like one who stretches out his hands toward water that it may reach his mouth, but it will not reach it.﴾ He likened the idols' response to those who worship them to the water's response to one who stretches out his palms toward it, and he indicated it by its approaching his mouth. On this reading, it never reaches his mouth, because water is inanimate and does not comprehend the intended purpose; likewise the idols. The pronoun in His saying "wa mā huwa" (and it is not) refers to the water, and the pronoun in "bi-bālighihi" (reaching it) refers to the mouth.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 13, verses 15–16:**

﴿To Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.﴾ The word *man* (من, "whoever") is only used for those who have reason, so here it refers to the angels, humankind and the jinn. If we take prostration (*sujud*) to mean submission to Allah's command and decree, then it is general to all of them, whether they believe or refuse. It is willing for those who submit and unwilling for those who reject and are angry. If we take prostration to be the known physical act, then it is the willing prostration of the angels and of the believers among humankind and the jinn. As for the unwilling, it is the prostration of the hypocrite (*munafiq*) and the prostration of the shadow of the disbeliever. ﴿And their shadows﴾ is coordinated with *man*, and the meaning is that the shadows prostrate morning and evening. Their prostration is their submission to being moved by the will of Allah, glory be to Him.

﴿Say: "Allah."﴾ This is an answer to the earlier question, which was "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" The answer and the question came from one side, because it is a clear matter that cannot be denied or disputed. For this reason, He established the proof against the polytheists with His words: ﴿Have you then taken besides Him protectors?﴾

﴿Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal?"﴾ The blind is a figure for the disbeliever, and the seeing is a figure for the believer. ﴿The darknesses﴾ are disbelief, and ﴿the light﴾ is faith. All of this is by way of comparison and illustration. ﴿Or have they set up for Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation became confused to them?⁠﴾ Here *am* (أم) means *bal* (بل, "rather") together with the interrogative hamza. *Khalaqu* (خلقوا, "they created") is a description of *shuraka'* (شركاء, "partners"). The meaning is that Allah confronted them [asked them]: have their partners created creations like the creation of Allah? That resemblance and confusion with what Allah created led them to take a god other than Allah. Then He nullified this with His words: ﴿Say: "Allah is the Creator of all things."﴾ Thus the refutation of them was achieved.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 17:

﴿He sent down water from the sky, and the valleys flowed according to their measure﴾ etc. This is a parable God struck for the Truth and its people, and for falsehood and its party. The likeness of the Truth and its people is the water that descends from the sky, by which the valleys flow and from which the people of the earth benefit, and [the likeness is also] gold, silver, iron, and copper (al-sufr, i.e. al-nuhas) and other metals from which people benefit. The falsehood is likened, in the swiftness of its dissipation and passing away, to the foam that the torrent carries upon it and that rises above those metals when they are melted, and there is no benefit in foam and it has no permanence. ﴿According to their measure﴾ may mean the measure of water decreed for them, and may mean according to what each can bear, in proportion to their smallness and largeness. ﴿Foam swelling high﴾: the foam is what the torrent carries of scum and the like, and "rabi" is the swollen, that which has risen, and from the same root comes "rabwa" (a raised height). ﴿And of that which they heat in the fire﴾: the prepositional phrase is in the position of the predicate preceding its subject, and the subject is "zabadun mithluhu" (foam like it): i.e., there arises from the things upon which they kindle fire a foam like the torrent's foam. ﴿Seeking ornament or utensils﴾: that which is heated in the fire seeking ornament is gold and silver, and that which is heated seeking utensils is iron, lead, copper, brass, and the like, and "mata'" (utensils) is what people enjoy in their households and needs. ﴿God strikes the Truth and falsehood﴾: i.e., He sets forth the likenesses of the Truth and falsehood. ﴿Cast away as scum﴾: which the torrent throws off, i.e., casts away. ﴿But as for that which benefits people, it remains in the earth﴾: meaning the pure water and the pure part of those metals.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 18:

﴿For those who responded to their Lord is the best (reward).﴾ "Those who responded" are the believers. This is a resumption of speech. Al-ḥusnā (the best) is Paradise. Its grammatical analysis (i'rab): al-ḥusnā is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "for those who responded." "Those who responded" is also a subject whose predicate is "even if they had whatever is on the earth..." (the verse that follows). Accordingly, one stops at "the parables" and at "al-ḥusnā." It has also been said that "for those who responded" is connected to "He strikes" (yaḍrib, i.e. "Allah sets forth the parables"), and al-ḥusnā is a verbal noun (maṣdar) derived from the sense of "responded," meaning: they responded with the best response. In that case "those who did not respond" is conjoined to "those who responded," and the meaning is: Allah sets forth the parables for the two groups. On this view one stops at "and those who did not respond to Him."

﴿Theirs will be the evil reckoning﴾, that is, the strict scrutiny and exhaustive accounting (al-munāqashah wa'l-istiqṣā').

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 19–24:

﴿Is he who knows﴾ is a rhetorical question (taqrir). The meaning is: is he who believes equal to he who does not believe? The blind one here is he who did not believe in the Prophet (ﷺ). "It was said: it was revealed concerning Hamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib (may Allah be pleased with him) and Abu Jahl (may Allah curse him)." ﴿who join together what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ — the ties of kinship and others. ﴿And who avert evil with good﴾ — it was said: they repel shirk with the statement "There is no god but Allah." It was also said: they repel those who wrong them with what is better. The more apparent meaning is that they do good deeds, and so they ward off evil deeds by them, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [Hud: 114]. It was also said: this verse was revealed concerning the Ansar, and then it is general for every believer who possesses these qualities. ﴿The final attainment of the home﴾ means Paradise. It may be that by "the home" is meant the Hereafter, and the "attainment" is attributed to it because it is in it; and it may be that by "the home" is meant the worldly life, and the "attainment" is attributed to it because it is its outcome. ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "the final attainment of the home," or the predicate of an implied subject, explaining "the final attainment of the home." ﴿And whoever was righteous﴾ — i.e., whoever was upright. ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ — i.e., they will say to them: "Peace be upon you." ﴿For what you patiently endured﴾ — it is connected to an implied element whose estimated form is: "This is because of what you endured patiently." It is also permissible for it to be connected to "peace," meaning: that peace be upon you because of what you endured patiently.

"It was said: it was revealed concerning Hamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib (may Allah be pleased with him) and Abu Jahl (may Allah curse him)." ﴿who join together what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ — the ties of kinship and others. ﴿And who avert evil with good﴾ — it was said: they repel shirk with the statement "There is no god but Allah." It was also said: they repel those who wrong them with what is better. The more apparent meaning is that they do good deeds, and so they ward off evil deeds by them, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [Hud: 114]. It was also said: this verse was revealed concerning the Ansar, and then it is general for every believer who possesses these qualities. ﴿The final attainment of the home﴾ means Paradise. It may be that by "the home" is meant the Hereafter, and the "attainment" is attributed to it because it is in it; and it may be that by "the home" is meant the worldly life, and the "attainment" is attributed to it because it is its outcome. ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "the final attainment of the home," or the predicate of an implied subject, explaining "the final attainment of the home." ﴿And whoever was righteous﴾ — i.e., whoever was upright. ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ — i.e., they will say to them: "Peace be upon you." ﴿For what you patiently endured﴾ — it is connected to an implied element whose estimated form is: "This is because of what you endured patiently." It is also permissible for it to be connected to "peace," meaning: that peace be upon you because of what you endured patiently.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 25:

﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah﴾ up to the end of the verse are descriptions that have been attached (to the earlier ones), as has already been mentioned. It has been said that they refer to the Khawarij, but the more apparent view is that they refer to the disbelievers. ﴿The evil abode﴾ may be understood to refer to both this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verses 26–29:

﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾. That is, He widens it for whom He wills and restricts it for whom He wills, and this is its explanation wherever it occurs. ﴿And they rejoice in the worldly life﴾. This is a report which contains within it a reproach and a declaration of the foolishness of those who rejoice in this world. Therefore He belittled it by saying: ﴿And the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is but a brief enjoyment﴾; that is, it is little when considered in relation to the Hereafter. ﴿Say: Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills﴾. This was stated in the manner of expressing wonder at them, since they asked for a sign. That is: Muhammad ﷺ has come to you with the Qur'an and many signs, yet you became blind to them, sought other than them, and persisted in disbelief, because Allah leaves astray whom He wills even when the signs are manifest, and He guides whom He wills apart from that. ﴿Those who believed, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah﴾. This is a substitute (badal) for "whoever turns back (man anab)", or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "those who believed and did righteous deeds"; or it is a second substitute, or it is the subject (mubtada'). ﴿Ṭūbā﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) from ṭāba, like bushrā, and its meaning is that they attained good and goodness. It was also said: it is a tree in Paradise, and its grammatical position (i'rab) is that of a subject (mubtada').

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 30:

﴿Thus We have sent you﴾ The kaf (the particle "thus") is connected to the meaning in His words: ﴿He sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [an-Nahl: 93]. ﴿While they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾ It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made a treaty with them in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and the scribe wrote "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Then one of them said: "We do not know the Most Merciful." But this is weak, because the verse was revealed before that, and because in that incident they only objected to the basmalah itself. The meaning of the verse is that they disbelieve in Allah while the Qur'an is being recited to them. ﴿Matab﴾ is on the pattern of mafʻal, derived from repentance (tawbah), and it is an ism al-masdar (a verbal noun used in place of the infinitive).

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (*al-Tashil*) on Surah 13, verse 31:**

﴿وَلَوْ أَنَّ قُرْآناً سُيِّرَتْ بِهِ ٱلْجِبَالُ﴾ ("And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains were set in motion…") **etc.:** The answer (*jawab*, the apodosis of *law*) is omitted. Its implied sense is: "If there were a Qur'an with this description, of moving the mountains, cleaving the earth and making the dead speak, they still would not believe in it." The meaning is like His saying: "They will not believe even if every sign comes to them." It was also said that the implied answer is: "If there were a Qur'an with this description, this Qur'an, which is the utmost in reminder and the final limit in warning, would be (sufficient)," like His saying: ﴿If We had sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split asunder﴾ [al-Hashr: 21]. It was also said that the clause is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: "They disbelieve in the All-Merciful, even if a Qur'an by which the mountains were set in motion…" ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَيْأَسِ﴾ ("Have those who believed not despaired…") means "Have they not known," and this is the dialect of Hawazin (a tribe). ﴿وَلاَ يَزَالُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ﴾ ("And those who disbelieve will not cease…") means the disbelievers of Quraysh. ﴿قَارِعَةٌ﴾ ("a calamity") means a disaster striking them in their persons, their children and their wealth, or the raids of the Muslims upon them. ﴿أَوْ تَحُلُّ﴾ ("or it settles close by"): the subject (*fa'il*, grammatical subject) is the pronoun referring to *al-qari'a* (the calamity). The meaning is either that it strikes them, or that it draws near to them. It was also said that the *ta'* (التاء) is for address (second person), and the subject is the pronoun of the addressee, who is the Prophet (ﷺ), but the first view is more apparent. ﴿حَتَّىٰ يَأْتِيَ وَعْدُ ٱللَّهِ﴾ ("until the promise of Allah comes"): it is the conquest of Makkah, and it was said it is the establishment of the Hour.

The commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verses 32–34:

﴿And certainly were messengers mocked﴾. Its purpose is to console and comfort the Prophet (ﷺ), and likewise wherever it occurs. ﴿Then I gave respite﴾, meaning I granted them a delay. ﴿Then is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾ is Allah, the Exalted, meaning the Guardian and Watcher over the deeds of every person. The predicate is omitted, and its intended meaning is: "Then is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned more deserving of being worshipped, or other than Him?" This is confirmed by His saying: "And they have made for Allah partners." ﴿Say, "Name them"﴾, meaning mention their names. ﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know on earth?﴾ The meaning is that Allah does not know of any partners for Himself, and if He does not know them, then they are nothing. So how do you fabricate lies in worshipping them and worship falsehood? This is like your saying, "Tell me, who is Zayd?" It is as if he is too insignificant to be known, so he is like nonexistence. ﴿Or [is it] by an apparent saying?﴾ The meaning is: do you name them partners merely by outward wording, without there being any reality to it? This is like His saying: ﴿They are not but names you have named, you and your forefathers﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. ﴿For them is a punishment in the worldly life﴾, meaning by killing, capture, fear, and other such things.

﴿The likeness of Paradise﴾. Here and in Surah Muhammad [15], it describes its attributes; it is not a parable (*darb mathal*) for it. According to Sibawayh, the predicate (*khabar*) is omitted and placed first, its implied sense being: "What is recited to you is the description of Paradise." Al-Farra' said the predicate comes after it, namely ﴿in which rivers flow beneath it﴾. ﴿Its fruit is constant﴾: meaning what is eaten therein, of fruits and other things. *Ukul* with a *damma* on the *hamza* means the food that is eaten. It may be read with a *damma* or a *sukun* on the *kaf*, while *akl* with a *fatha* on the *hamza* is the verbal noun.

﴿And those to whom We gave the Scripture rejoice in what has been sent down to you﴾: meaning those among the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and al-Najashi and his companions. It was also said: it means the believers, and "the Scripture" in this case is the Qur'an.

﴿And among the factions﴾: it was said they are the Banu Umayyah and the Banu al-Mughirah of Quraysh. The more evident view is that it refers to all the disbelievers of the Arabs. It was also said they are the Jews and Christians, because they do not deny the stories (*qisas*) and the matters that are in their books; they only deny some of what they do not recognize or have distorted.

﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship Allah﴾: the connection with what precedes is that it is a response to the deniers; it refuts them, as if he said: I have only been commanded to worship Allah and affirm His oneness, so how can you deny this?

*Ma'ab*: it is on the pattern *maf'al* from *al-awb*, which means return. That is, my return in the Hereafter, or my return through repentance.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 38:

﴿And We did make for them wives and offspring.﴾ This is a refutation of those who denied that the Messenger could be a human being, or that he could need what human beings need, such as wives and offspring. The meaning is: you are not unprecedented in this; rather, you are like those Messengers who came before you.

﴿And it was not for a Messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah.﴾ This is a refutation of those who demanded signs. ﴿For every term there is a Book.﴾ Al-Farra' (al-Farra') said: "For every Book there is a term," in reverse. This does not necessarily follow; rather, the meaning is correct without reversal, i.e., for every term there is a Book which Allah has written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 13, verse 39:

﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes [what He wills].﴾ It has been said: this means He abrogates (naskh) whatever He wills of the Qur'an and of the rulings, and establishes whatever He wills of them. It has also been said: it refers to the terms (ajal) of the children of Adam. This is because Allah, exalted is He, decrees in the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr), and it has been said: in the night of the middle of Sha'ban, the writing down of the term of whoever will die in that year; so He erases him from the register of the living, and establishes whoever will not die in that year. It has also been said: the effacing and establishing is general, applying to all things. But this is rejected by the established principle that decree is not changed and that Allah's knowledge does not alter. Some of them said: the effacing and establishing applies to everything except happiness and misery in the Hereafter, and [except] the terms. ﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾: the origin of every book, and it is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), in which Allah has written the destinies of all things.

﴿وَإِن مَّا نُرِيَنَّكَ﴾ *In* (إن), a conditional particle, is followed by *ma* (ما), which is the emphatic (المؤكدة) *ma*. Its answer (جوابها) is *fa-innama* (فإنما): ﴿so it is only (فإنما) ...﴾.

﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْاْ أَنَّا نَأْتِي ٱلأَرْضَ نَنقُصُهَا مِنْ أَطْرَافِهَا﴾ *Have they not seen that We come to the land, reducing it from its edges?* The coming (الاتيان) here means coming by power and command. "The land" is the land of the disbelievers, and its reduction is by what Allah opens to the Muslims from it. The meaning is: *Or have they not seen that, so that they fear We may give you power over them?* It was also said: "the land" is a generic noun (جنس), and its reduction is by the death of people, the destruction of crops, the ruin of towns, and the like.
